cards.front: Why is a plant cell firm when its large central vacuole is full of water?
cards.back: The full vacuole (the water tank) pushes the cell out against the cell wall (the box). The wall pushes back, so the cell is firm.
cards.quote: When the tank is full, it pushes the cell out against the box, the box pushes back, and the cell is firm.

cards.front: Water pressure holds up celery stalks and leaves. What mainly holds up a woody tree trunk?
cards.back: Thick, hard cell walls. They keep holding the trunk up even after the cells inside them die.
cards.quote: A woody tree trunk stands mainly on thick, hard cell walls.

cards.front: Why does water pressure not hold up your body the way it holds up a celery stalk?
cards.back: Your cells have no cell wall for the water to push against. Your skeleton holds you up instead.
cards.quote: Your cells have the shared kit but no box, so water does not hold you up; your skeleton does.

cards.front: A micrometre (µm) is one {{c1::thousandth}} of a millimetre.
cards.quote: One check below uses the micrometre (µm), one thousandth of a millimetre.

cards.front: A model plant cell has a cell wall and chloroplasts and plenty of water, but no large central vacuole. Predict how stiff it is, and say why.
cards.back: Less stiff than a cell with a full tank. Firmness comes from a full tank pushing the cell out against the wall, and here there is no tank to push.
cards.quote: What if the box is there but the tank is not?
cards.section: Explore: build a cell for a job

cards.front: A model plant cell keeps its chloroplasts, but the light is turned off. Predict how much food it makes, and say why.
cards.back: Little or none. Chloroplasts use the energy in light to make sugar, so with no light they cannot make food.
cards.quote: Turn the light off but keep the chloroplasts on. Predict the food bar.
cards.section: Explore: build a cell for a job

cards.front: Name the six kinds of parts that plant cells and animal cells share.
cards.back: Nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and vacuoles.
cards.quote: Key idea: Plant and animal cells share a nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and vacuoles.
cards.section: Explain: the parts all these cells share

cards.front: The {{c1::nucleus}} holds the cell's DNA, its instructions, and controls what the cell does.
cards.quote: The nucleus holds the cell's DNA, its instructions, and controls what the cell does.
cards.section: Explain: the parts all these cells share

cards.front: The {{c1::cell membrane}} is a thin outer layer that controls what goes in and out of the cell.
cards.quote: The cell membrane is a thin outer layer that controls what goes in and out.
cards.section: Explain: the parts all these cells share

cards.front: The {{c1::mitochondria}} release energy from sugar (glucose) in a form the cell can use.
cards.quote: The mitochondria release energy from sugar (glucose) in a form the cell can use.
cards.section: Explain: the parts all these cells share

cards.front: Name the three parts plant cells add that animal cells lack, and the job of each.
cards.back: Cell wall: supports and protects the cell. Chloroplasts: capture the energy in light to make food. Large central vacuole: stores water and, when full, pushes the cell against the wall.
cards.quote: Key idea: Plant cells add a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole.

cards.front: Why do green plant cells need mitochondria if they already have chloroplasts?
cards.back: Chloroplasts make sugar using light. Mitochondria release energy from that sugar, day and night. The two parts do different jobs.
cards.quote: Plant cells have mitochondria too, so they can release energy from that sugar, day and night.

cards.front: A full onion skin cell pushes out far harder than the air in a party balloon. Why does the cell not burst?
cards.back: The stiff cell wall holds it in. A balloon has no wall around it, so it would burst at that pressure.
cards.why: Measured with a fine probe, the onion cell's push was about three times the extra pressure pumped into a car tyre.
cards.quote: A party balloon could never push that hard without bursting; the plant cell can because the wall holds it in.

cards.front: Give two ways a real plant cell differs from the balloon-in-a-box model.
cards.back: A real wall can stretch a little, and water moves in and out of a real cell all the time.
cards.quote: A real wall can stretch a little, and water moves in and out of a cell all the time.

cards.front: A cell comes from a plant root growing in dark soil. Predict whether it has chloroplasts, a cell wall and mitochondria.
cards.back: Usually no chloroplasts, because their job needs light. It still has a cell wall, and mitochondria to release energy from sugar.
cards.quote: Cells that get no light, like most root cells and onion bulb cells, usually have no chloroplasts.

cards.front: Under a microscope, why do plant cells often have straight sides while animal cells look rounder or flatter?
cards.back: The stiff cell wall gives plant cells straight sides. Animal cells have no wall.
cards.quote: Shape fits too: the wall gives plant cells straight sides, while animal cells are often rounder or flatter.

cards.front: About 18 human cheek cells laid side by side span one millimetre (1,000 µm). About how wide is one cheek cell?
cards.back: 1,000 µm ÷ 18 = about 56 µm, close to the 55 µm a study measured.
cards.quote: About 18 human cheek cells laid side by side would span one millimetre on a ruler.

cards.front: In a table of real cell measurements, which two plant cells show that not every plant cell has chloroplasts?
cards.back: Onion bulb skin cells and the colorless waterweed leaf cells. Both are plant cells with no chloroplasts.
cards.quote: Which rows show that not every plant cell has chloroplasts?

cards.front: Most plant and animal cells have a nucleus. Name one kind of cell that does not.
cards.back: Mature red blood cells in mammals.
cards.quote: Most plant and animal cells have a nucleus, but a few do not: mature red blood cells in mammals have none, as the table shows.

cards.front: A class tests whether limp celery gets firmer when it stands in water. What is the control group, and what do they measure?
cards.back: Control: stalks in empty cups, measured the same way. They measure how far each stalk bends, in centimetres, with a 20-gram mass hung on the thin end.
cards.quote: Control: stalks in empty cups, measured the same way.

cards.front: A potted plant is not watered for days. Its leaves droop, but the woody stem of a nearby tree stays upright. Explain both, then predict what happens when the plant is watered.
cards.back: Leaves droop because their vacuoles lose water and stop pushing against the walls. The trunk stands on thick, hard walls, not water pressure. After watering, vacuoles refill and the leaves firm up again.
cards.why: Rests on two rules: water pressure holds up soft parts; thick walls hold up woody trunks.
cards.quote: Water pressure holds up soft plant parts, like celery stalks, leaves and young stems.

cards.front: A cell under a microscope has straight sides and a large central vacuole but no chloroplasts. Is it a plant or animal cell, and what might explain the missing chloroplasts?
cards.back: A plant cell: the wall gives straight sides, and the big tank is a plant part. It likely gets little or no light, like a root or onion bulb cell, though light is not the whole story.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a cell's parts most often fit its job.
cards.quote: A cell's parts most often fit its job, and a chloroplast's job needs light.
